newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk Opel won't lay off despite car sector crisis.
newsitem.headline: Turk Opel won't lay off despite car sector crisis.

text.p: Opel Turkey, a subsidiary of the German-U.S. carmaker Adam Opel, does not plan any lay-offs despite a shrinkage in the Turkish automobile sector, its general manager said on Friday.
"Despite all inconveniences, we don't plan to lay off any workers," Kevin Jackson, general manager of Opel Turkey, told Reuters.

The local car industry has been in the doldrums after the government decided in September to allow Turkish residents and expatriates to import one duty-free foreign car under five years of age for each 50,000 marks they deposit by end-1996 at public Ziraat Bank for one year.

This has led to a growing dispute between the government and local car industrialists and trade unions which say the scheme will undermine the sector, which employs about 450,000 people including spare parts producers.
Jackson said the scheme was causing uncertainty in the producers and investors.
"Nobody knows what is going to happen. The decree (on car import scheme) is harming the local industries," he said.
He said he feared many stolen or damaged cars would be imported under the plan, which the government said was aimed at partly financing deficits.

Turkey's biggest car maker, Tofas Turk Otomobil Fabrikasi, responded to counter the car import scheme by putting its 4,500 workers on compulsory leaves until next Tuesday after capacity fell below 40 percent at its Bursa plant.
The company, a partnership between Italy's Fiat and Turkish conglomerate Koc Holding, will also cut production to two shifts from three next week and lay off 1,011 workers from January.
Officials said the car import plan has so far raised about $110 million, with applications to bring in 2,015 duty free cars.
Industry Minister Yalim Erez said on Thursday Tofas' decision to lay off workers was untimely and not necessary.
"If there was really a crisis in he sector, Renault and Opel would also have laid off workers," he said.

Turkey's car output slumped by 26 percent in September to 18,540 compared to the same 1995 month as demand fell over duty-free import plan. Car sales stood at 17,500 in September, down 25 percent from September 1995.
Jackson said Opel's market share rose to 10.8 percent in 1995 from 4.4 percent a year ago.
"We plan to raise our market share to 12 percent next year, when we put out our Sintra sports model," he said.

Opel Turkey, set up in 1990, has a production capacity of 15,000 units per year and assembles Vectra and Astra models. It made 6,626 cars in 1995 and the output in the first 10 months of 1996 was 8,548 cars, compared to 6,456 in the same 1995 period.
It employs about 300 workers at its plant near western Izmir city and is the fourth biggest car maker in Turkey after Tofas, Oyak-Renault and ToyotaSa.
